result_text:
The rate limiters now choose their headers based on the HTTP method. A GET request uses Strava's new read-rate-limit headers (`X-ReadRateLimit-Usage` and `X-ReadRateLimit-Limit`). Every other method keeps using `X-RateLimit-*`.

If a GET response has no read-limit headers, it falls back to the overall `X-RateLimit-*` headers, so current Strava behaviour is unchanged. I did not run it against real Strava responses, and I did not add tests, per your instructions.

Test status: 38 tests fail in `src/stravalib/tests`, and the same 38 fail without my change. I didn't look into why.

Changes:
- **`protocol.py`:** the request now passes its method to the rate limiter, as `rate_limiter(raw.headers, method)`.
- **`util/limiter.py`:**
  - `get_rates_from_response_headers` takes a `method` argument, defaulting to `"GET"`.
  - `XRateLimitRule`, `SleepingRateLimitRule`, `RateLimitRule` and `RateLimiter` accept an optional `method` argument.

Custom rate limiters passed to `Protocol` now need to accept `(headers, method)`. The built-in ones default `method` to `"GET"`, so direct calls like `rule(headers)` still work.

I didn't go further than the headers. Each rule still tracks one short and one long window. It does not keep separate read and non-read counters, so mixed GET and non-GET traffic share the same tracked state.
